questions.q: What is the difference between an event publishing allocation and an event delivery allocation?
options: They are the same allocation under two different names
Delivery allocation only applies to Apex triggers, never to CometD or Pub/Sub API clients
Publishing allocation only applies to standard-volume events
Publishing allocation caps how many events can be published; delivery allocation caps how many can be delivered to subscribing clients, shared across all clients in a 24-hour period
questions.explain: These are two distinct allocations: one caps publishing volume, the other caps delivery to subscribing clients (Pub/Sub API, CometD, empApi, event relays) within a rolling 24-hour window shared across all of an org's clients.

questions.q: Why does this lesson avoid stating one fixed number for the event delivery allocation?
options: Because platform events have no delivery allocation at all
Because delivery allocations were removed in the most recent release
Because the allocation scales by Salesforce edition and by add-on entitlements an org can purchase, so the current Platform Event Allocations page is the authoritative source
Because only Developer Edition orgs have a delivery allocation
questions.explain: The exact allocation varies by edition and by purchasable add-on entitlements, so the lesson teaches the shape of the limit and points to Salesforce's own current allocations documentation rather than a number that could become outdated.

questions.q: What happens to events generated after an org exceeds its delivery allocation?
options: They are permanently lost and cannot be recovered
The org is automatically upgraded to a higher edition
All platform events in the org are disabled until the next release
They are still stored on the event bus and can be retrieved later, within the retention window, once allocation is available again
questions.explain: Exceeding the delivery allocation doesn't discard events outright — they remain stored on the event bus and can be retrieved later within the normal retention window, though delivery may be delayed.

questions.q: What does a publish callback (`EventBus.EventPublishSuccessCallback` / `FailureCallback`) tell you that a `Database.SaveResult` alone does not?
options: The field values of every subscriber's record updates
Whether the subscribing Apex trigger threw an exception
The final outcome of the asynchronous publish operation, rather than just confirmation that the event was queued
The exact Replay ID a future subscriber should use
questions.explain: A Database.SaveResult from EventBus.publish() only confirms the event was queued. A publish callback's onSuccess/onFailure methods report the actual final outcome once the platform finishes the publish attempt.

questions.q: Why is 'the publish call returned success' not sufficient evidence that an event-driven pipeline fully worked?
options: Because publish calls always fail silently with no way to detect it
Because EventBus.publish() cannot be called more than once per transaction
Because only CDC events need separate subscriber-side monitoring
Because publish success only confirms queuing or final publish outcome — it says nothing about whether a specific downstream subscriber actually received and processed the event
questions.explain: Publishing success (even confirmed via a callback) only tells you the event left the publisher successfully — confirming a specific subscriber actually processed it requires separate tracking on the subscriber side, such as the Lesson 10 tracking-record pattern.
